sites.title: Athens
sites.body: High above Athens, the Parthenon was built for Athena. Its sculptures and columns still shape how we imagine ancient Greece.
sites.question: What might a city's buildings say about its values?
sites.gullLine: A temple for Athena. An excellent lookout for a gull.
sites.imageAlt: A wide view of the Parthenon on the Acropolis
sites.caption: The Parthenon · Acropolis, Athens

sites.title: Pompeii
sites.body: Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79. Its houses, shops and wall paintings offer remarkable evidence of everyday Roman life.
sites.question: What would archaeologists learn from your room?
sites.gullLine: Shops, baths, streets… I am still looking for the chip shop.
sites.imageAlt: The forum at Pompeii with Mount Vesuvius in the distance
sites.caption: The forum · Pompeii, Italy

sites.title: Delphi
sites.body: People travelled to Delphi to consult Apollo's oracle. Religion, politics and difficult decisions met in this mountain sanctuary.
sites.question: Who do you turn to when the answer is uncertain?
sites.gullLine: I asked the oracle about lunch. The answer was mysterious.
sites.imageAlt: The circular Tholos among the ruins of Delphi
sites.caption: The Tholos · Delphi, Greece

sites.title: Rome
sites.body: The Colosseum brings us face to face with Roman entertainment, public spectacle and power. Its scale still dominates the city.
sites.question: What does entertainment reveal about a society?
sites.gullLine: So many seats. Surely someone brought a sandwich.
sites.imageAlt: The arches of the Colosseum in Rome
sites.caption: The Colosseum · Rome, Italy

sites.title: Ephesus
sites.period: A city of the Roman world
sites.body: The Library of Celsus is one of Ephesus's great Roman monuments. This former port city connected people and ideas across the Mediterranean.
sites.question: Why might a city make its library so impressive?
sites.gullLine: A library! At last, somewhere to research local seafood.
sites.imageAlt: The monumental façade of the Library of Celsus at Ephesus
sites.caption: The Library of Celsus · Ephesus, Türkiye

sites.title: Bath
sites.body: Hot springs made Bath a place for bathing, healing and worship. The surviving baths reveal how Roman engineering shaped daily life.
sites.question: What would you include in a building designed for everyone?
sites.gullLine: A heated pool. I shall leave the swimming to the Romans.
sites.caption: The Great Bath · Bath, England

sites.title: Hadrian’s Wall
sites.landmark: At the edge of an empire
sites.body: Hadrian’s Wall crossed northern Britain, linking forts and settlements. Its remains help us explore how Rome organised and controlled a frontier.
sites.question: Does a border divide people, connect them, or both?
sites.gullLine: A very long wall. Fortunately, I can fly over it.
sites.caption: Hadrian’s Wall · northern England
sites.sourceLabel: UNESCO · Frontiers of the Roman Empire

sites.title: Pont du Gard
sites.body: Three tiers of Roman arches carried an aqueduct across the river. Bringing water to a city demanded careful planning as well as impressive construction.
sites.question: Which everyday service would your town struggle without?
sites.gullLine: All that engineering, and not a single drinking fountain for gulls.
sites.caption: Pont du Gard · southern France

sites.title: Paestum
sites.body: The temples at Paestum are a reminder that the Greek world stretched beyond modern Greece. This landscape brought different Mediterranean cultures into contact.
sites.question: How do buildings preserve the identity of a community?
sites.gullLine: These columns have been standing much longer than I have been flying.
sites.caption: Greek temples · Paestum, Italy

sites.title: Olympia
sites.period: Home of the ancient Olympic Games
sites.body: Temples and sporting spaces stood together at Olympia. The ancient Olympic Games belonged to a religious festival, bringing competitors to the sanctuary of Zeus.
sites.question: What do modern sporting events share with ancient festivals?
sites.gullLine: I have entered the flying event. Apparently, it is not on the programme.
sites.caption: The sanctuary · Olympia, Greece

sites.title: Knossos
sites.body: Knossos was a major palace centre long before the Parthenon was built. Its rooms, courts and storerooms offer evidence of a complex Bronze Age society.
sites.question: What can the layout of a palace tell us about power?
sites.gullLine: So many rooms. I should have brought a ball of string.
sites.imageAlt: Columns and remains at the palace of Knossos
sites.caption: Palace remains · Knossos, Crete

sites.title: Jerash
sites.landmark: A Roman city in the east
sites.body: Colonnaded streets, theatres and public spaces survive at Jerash. This city shows how Roman urban life developed far beyond Italy.
sites.question: What makes a collection of buildings feel like a city?
sites.gullLine: A whole plaza of columns. Plenty of room for a dramatic entrance.
sites.caption: The Oval Plaza · Jerash, Jordan

sites.title: Segovia
sites.body: Two tiers of stone arches carried water into Segovia. The aqueduct still shapes the city, showing how practical infrastructure can become a landmark.
sites.question: When does a useful structure become a work of art?
sites.gullLine: An excellent row of perches. The water supply was a useful extra.
sites.caption: Roman aqueduct · Segovia, Spain

sites.title: Orange
sites.body: The theatre at Orange preserves a remarkable Roman stage wall. Its design makes us think about performance, audiences and the place of entertainment in city life.
sites.question: How does the space change the way we experience a performance?
sites.gullLine: I have tested the acoustics. Everyone heard me.
sites.caption: The Roman theatre · Orange, France

sites.title: Leptis Magna
sites.body: The streets, theatre and public buildings of Leptis Magna reveal a major Roman city in North Africa. Rome’s history reaches across the Mediterranean.
sites.question: How might trade change the fortunes of a city?
sites.gullLine: A theatre with a sea view. I approve of the location.
sites.caption: The theatre · Leptis Magna, Libya
sites.sourceLabel: UNESCO · Archaeological Site of Leptis Magna

people.title: Tom Hiddleston
people.body: Known for playing Loki in the Marvel films and for leading roles on stage and television. He studied Classics before training at RADA.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Tom Hiddleston

people.title: Chris Martin
people.body: Coldplay’s singer and co-founder studied Greek and Latin at university, where the band’s members met.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Chris Martin

people.title: Anthony Leggett
people.body: After his Classics degree he took a second degree in physics. He shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on superconductors and superfluids.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Anthony Leggett

people.title: Madeline Miller
people.connection: BA and MA in Classics · Brown University
people.body: Author of The Song of Achilles and Circe. Her first novel won the Orange Prize for Fiction, bringing ancient stories to a new readership.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Madeline Miller

people.title: Oscar Wilde
people.connection: Classics · Trinity College Dublin and Oxford
people.body: Author of The Importance of Being Earnest and The Picture of Dorian Gray. His classical studies preceded a celebrated literary career.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Oscar Wilde

people.title: C. S. Lewis
people.body: The author of The Chronicles of Narnia gained a first in Classics, then another in English, before his career as a writer and scholar.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: C. S. Lewis
people.sourceLabel: University College, Oxford · C. S. Lewis

people.title: Charlotte Higgins
people.body: The Guardian’s chief culture writer and an award-winning author. Her work ranges from Greek mythology to reporting on art and culture.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.imageAlt: CH: original name graphic for Charlotte Higgins
people.caption: Charlotte Higgins · name graphic

people.title: Edith Hall
people.body: An award-winning scholar of Greek literature who also advises theatre companies and campaigns to widen access to classical subjects.
people.question: Where might your interest in the ancient world take you?
people.caption: Edith Hall

people.title: Natalie Haynes
people.body: Novelist and broadcaster whose books and radio programmes bring Greek myths and their characters to new audiences.
people.question: How does a story change when someone else tells it?
people.caption: Natalie Haynes · writer and broadcaster

people.title: Mary Beard
people.body: Historian, bestselling author and television presenter whose work has brought ancient Rome to a wide public.
people.question: Whose voices survive from the Roman world?
people.caption: Mary Beard · filming in Rome

careers.title: Law
careers.body: Weigh competing accounts, spot the detail that matters and explain a case clearly. These are habits you practise when studying ancient texts.
careers.challenge: Two witnesses disagree. How would you test their accounts?
careers.note: A possible route; professional training and entry requirements apply.

careers.title: Journalism
careers.lead:
Question the source.
Tell the story.
careers.body: Ask who wrote an account, what they wanted readers to believe and which voices are missing. The same questions matter in reporting.
careers.challenge: What would you check before publishing a dramatic claim?
careers.note: A possible route; experience and further training may be needed.

careers.title: Museums & heritage
careers.lead:
Study the object.
Share its story.
careers.body: Use objects, texts and places to explore how people lived. Then help other people understand the evidence and its limits.
careers.challenge: Which object would you choose to explain life in Eastbourne?
careers.note: A possible route; specialist roles often need further study or training.

careers.title: Publishing
careers.lead:
Find the meaning.
Choose the words.
careers.body: Translation and literary study involve careful choices about language, audience and meaning. Those habits can help in editing and publishing.
careers.challenge: Can you make a complicated idea clear without losing its meaning?
careers.note: A possible route; experience and role-specific training may be needed.

careers.title: Technology
careers.lead:
Spot the pattern.
Solve the problem.
careers.body: Working through grammar and translation develops patient, structured problem-solving. Combine those habits with the technical skills a role requires.
careers.challenge: What small rule might explain a complicated pattern?
careers.note: A possible route; technical roles need additional technical skills.

careers.title: Diplomacy
careers.body: Studying societies with different values asks you to listen carefully and question assumptions. Those habits matter when people negotiate across cultures.
careers.challenge: Two groups want different things. Where could an agreement begin?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Public policy
careers.lead:
Test the evidence.
Consider the effects.
careers.body: Ancient history asks how decisions affect communities. Policy work also involves weighing evidence, understanding institutions and explaining choices.
careers.challenge: How would you judge whether a new rule had worked?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Finance
careers.lead:
Read the detail.
Assess the risk.
careers.body: A difficult passage demands accuracy and patience. In finance, combine these habits with the numerical knowledge and professional training the role requires.
careers.challenge: What would you need to know before trusting a confident prediction?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Business & consulting
careers.lead:
Ask better questions.
Make a clear case.
careers.body: Comparing interpretations helps you identify a problem, test an explanation and present a reasoned recommendation. Businesses need these habits too.
careers.challenge: A plan sounds convincing. What evidence would make you question it?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Teaching
careers.lead:
Make it clear.
Help others think.
careers.body: Explaining a translation or a historical argument means noticing where understanding breaks down. Teachers use that attention to help pupils make progress.
careers.challenge: How would you explain an unfamiliar idea to a younger pupil?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Film & theatre
careers.lead:
Read the character.
Imagine the scene.
careers.body: Greek and Roman drama asks how words, motives and performance work together. These questions can lead into acting, directing, writing and production.
careers.challenge: How could two actors make the same line mean different things?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Marketing
careers.lead:
Know the audience.
Choose the message.
careers.body: Ancient speeches show how speakers try to persuade. Examining their methods helps you think critically about communication, audience and trust.
careers.challenge: What makes a persuasive message fair as well as effective?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Archaeology
careers.lead:
Find the trace.
Test the explanation.
careers.body: Objects, inscriptions and buildings offer different kinds of evidence. Archaeologists combine them to investigate the past and explain what remains uncertain.
careers.challenge: What could a broken object tell you that a written account cannot?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

careers.title: Translation
careers.lead:
Hear the voice.
Carry the meaning.
careers.body: Every translation involves choices about tone, context and audience. Professional language work combines these habits with advanced knowledge of relevant languages.
careers.challenge: When is a word-for-word translation less accurate?
careers.note: A possible route; relevant qualifications, experience or specialist training may be needed.

news.title:
A blue room
in Pompeii
news.body: Excavators uncovered a room painted in blue, a colour rarely found in Pompeian frescoes. They interpret it as a space for ritual activities and sacred objects.
news.why: Wall paintings can reveal how Romans used a room, as well as how they decorated it.
news.imageAlt: Pompeii's forum and Vesuvius, shown as a location photograph
news.caption: Location photograph: Pompeii's forum; not the excavated room

news.title:
Roman pizza?
Look again.
news.body: A Pompeian painting of bread with toppings prompted comparisons with pizza. The scene includes fruit and wine, but it is not evidence of modern tomato-and-mozzarella pizza.
news.why: A familiar-looking object can tempt us to read modern habits into ancient evidence.
news.imageAlt: Pompeii's forum, shown as a location photograph for the fresco story
news.caption: Location photograph: Pompeii's forum; not the wall painting
news.sourceLabel: Archaeology magazine · Archaeological Institute of America

news.title:
Inside a Roman
household cupboard
news.body: A cupboard excavated in Pompeii contained personal-care objects, vessels and small amulets. The finds offer a detailed glimpse of domestic life before the eruption of AD 79.
news.why: Small household objects can reveal routines and beliefs that grand monuments leave out.
news.imageAlt: Location photograph of Pompeii, not the reported finds
news.caption: Location photograph: Pompeii’s forum; not the discovery
news.sourceLabel: Archaeological Park of Pompeii · excavation journal

news.title:
Looking beneath
a buried villa
news.body: A geophysical survey at Pompeii’s so-called Villa of Cicero detected traces consistent with buried structures and earlier excavations. The results are preliminary.
news.why: Archaeologists can investigate a buried site without immediately digging it up.
news.imageAlt: Location photograph of Pompeii, not the reported finds
news.caption: Location photograph: Pompeii’s forum; not the discovery
news.sourceLabel: Archaeological Park of Pompeii · excavation journal
